conversation_lines.text: Ah, right. Because of the risk of trapping an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve sent stool tests for C. diff, norovirus, and other infections. All came back negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my kidney numbers? I know they’ve been up before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.5, which is a bit higher than your baseline, so we’re watching for acute kidney injury on top of your chronic kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s usually around 1.1. But it’s bounced between 1.5 and 2 before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, so we’ll keep monitoring it daily. We’ve given you 3 liters of IV fluids to help with dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit dry. My mouth’s been parched.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your exam showed dry mucous membranes. We’ll keep you on IV fluids until you can tolerate sips and we’re sure you’re rehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips. If you keep those down, we’ll slowly advance your diet. Nutrition is consulting to help plan your G-tube feeds once you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually rely on the G-tube for most of my calories. But I’m so nauseous, I didn’t think I could handle feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re holding off for now. We don’t want to worsen the nausea. But we’ll reassess daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I kept down some apple juice last night. Still nauseous, but not vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We did an ultrasound of your liver this morning—everything looks stable. Hepatic vessels are patent, no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any sign of bile duct problems or infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bile duct is mildly dilated at 1.1 cm, but that’s unchanged from before. No signs of obstruction or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my CMV? I’ve had colitis from that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV IgM is negative, and viral load is undetectable. No sign of reactivation. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent cultures for salmonella, shigella, campylobacter—all negative. So it looks like viral gastroenteritis, likely from the flu.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no bacteria or parasites?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And your lipase was normal, so we’re not worried about pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I try more food today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, let’s try clear liquids and see how you do. We’ll advance slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs show your white count and hemoglobin are down a bit, but stable. Creatinine is holding at 1.6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. Your pancytopenia is chronic, so this may just be your baseline. But we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on darbepoetin for that. Should I restart it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss with your transplant team. For now, focus on recovering your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had only three bowel movements today. Closer to my usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Since your cultures are negative, we’ll restart your loperamide and opium tincture as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel like I’m turning a corner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been tolerating a soft diet, and your vitals are stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home meds, including the Tamiflu for the full 10 days. Restart your G-tube feeds as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pending blood and stool cultures?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those will keep being monitored. If anything comes back positive, we’ll let you know. But so far, everything points to viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I follow up with my transplant doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. And your primary care provider to review your labs and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home today. You look much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot better. Still weak, but the nausea is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep taking the Tamiflu, advance your diet slowly, and monitor for any return of symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? Can I go back to my usual doses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume all your home medications as listed in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted for nausea and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your mycophenolate, prednisone, and pain meds. We’re avoiding Zofran for nausea because of your long QT, but Ativan is helping and is safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, my heart condition. I’ve had torsades before. So no Zofran—got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your blood cultures came back clean. No bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture grew Proteus mirabilis, which matches your earlier UTIs. It’s sensitive to Bactrim, which you’ve tolerated before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home with a 7-day course of Bactrim. Even though you finished one recently, this ensures the infection clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave a small dose of IV ceftriaxone earlier, but you developed itching in your hands. We gave Benadryl, and it’s improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my hands got really itchy. Is that an allergy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You’re already allergic to penicillins and ciprofloxacin, so we’ll note ceftriaxone as a possible allergy. We’ll avoid it in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had reactions before. What about the rash on my neck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s faint and improving. Could be related to the ceftriaxone or just a mild skin reaction. Keep an eye on it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look much better. Creatinine is down to 1.6—back to your baseline. You’ve kept down food and fluids well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you. You’ll finish the Bactrim at home, and we’ll send instructions for follow-up urine tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart my G-tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Nutrition recommends continuing your usual feeds. If you eat less than half your normal amount by mouth, give one can of 2-calorie formula through the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my heart—should I get an EKG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your doctor will order a follow-up EKG to check your QT interval. Avoid any medications that can prolong it until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better. I’ll follow up with my transplant and primary care teams.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. Take care, and call if you have any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve had this constant pain near my belly button for about two days now. And I’ve had five loose stools today—no blood, but it’s worse than my usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice—dark green vomit. I couldn’t keep my meds down yesterday, including my transplant pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chest pain. Just the belly pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of C. diff and liver transplant, we need to be careful. We’ve started some fluids and gave you Zofran for nausea. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had C. diff before. This feels similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re checking your stool. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen to rule out blockages or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the CT safe with my heart condition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. We avoid certain medications due to your long QT, but imaging is fine. The scan showed no blockage or perforation—your transplant liver looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. My G-tube has been clogged too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Nutrition is helping with Ensure for now. We’ll plan to replace the tube if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My blood pressure’s usually okay—why is it so high now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from pain and stress. We’ll monitor it. If it stays high, we may start a mild medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back positive for C. diff—both the PCR and toxin tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s what’s causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Even though the CT didn’t show colitis, the positive toxin means we should treat it. We’re starting oral vancomycin—125 mg four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that interact with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s safe with your transplant meds. We’ve held loperamide and opium tincture for now—they can worsen C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll skip those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up to 2.4—likely from not eating or drinking much. We’re giving some IV fluids to help your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney damage getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like temporary stress from dehydration. Your levels were 1.5 on admission and should improve with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on Ensure—will I get tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend it, but you can decide. We’ll replace the clogged tube soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving, and you’re keeping food down. Creatinine is already down to 1.8—great response to fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interventional radiology will replace it tomorrow. It’s a quick procedure under light sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be drowsy but breathing on your own. We’ll use medications safe for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray shows a small fluid collection on the right side—likely from reduced movement. It’s not pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s common in hospitalized patients. Deep breathing and walking will help clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. You need to finish a few more days of vancomycin. We also want to make sure your blood pressure stays down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, consistently above 150. We’re starting amlodipine 5 mg daily. Your PCP will adjust it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your G-tube was successfully replaced this morning. It’s ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it go well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The old tube was damaged, which caused the clog. The new one is secure. Home health will help with feeds after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try feeds at home, but I’m not sure I want them long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ll support whatever you choose. Nutrition will send instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last labs show creatinine back to 1.5, and you’re tolerating food. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds do I take home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds except loperamide and opium tincture—they stay on hold. Add vancomycin for 14 days and amlodipine daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can restart feeds at home. A nurse will visit to help set it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Keep taking vancomycin until the end of the course, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any warning signs to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call if diarrhea returns severely, or if you have fever, belly swelling, or can’t keep fluids down. Also monitor your weight—call if you gain or lose more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—avoid QT-prolonging drugs. Your PCP may check an EKG in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your team soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one more thing—should I restart my pain meds fully?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue oxymorphone and hydromorphone as needed. Use the lidocaine patch and gabapentin too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—keep taking mycophenolate and prednisone every day. Do not skip them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—vancomycin four times a day, amlodipine once daily, and no loperamide until diarrhea resolves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And weigh yourself daily, low-salt diet, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can I start by confirming your name?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s James. I’ve been having really bad stomach pain and vomiting for the past three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The nurse told me it started around your belly button and feels burning. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It hasn’t moved, but it’s constant. And I’ve thrown up maybe 20 times—mostly just water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel chilly, but I haven’t checked my temperature.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And your stools—have they changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they’ve always been loose because of my colon surgery, but now they’re even more watery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We ran some tests. Your white blood cell count is up, which suggests infection. We also did a CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it my C. diff again? I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on the stool test, but the CT showed something else too. Your feeding tube is coiled back in the stomach and not in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I haven’t been using it much, but my nurse helps me when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely contributing to the nausea and vomiting. We’ll need to fix that. Also, your kidney function is a bit off—your creatinine is 1.5, which is slightly elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s not good. I have CKD, so I worry about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV fluids to help. And we’re starting you on antibiotics for possible C. diff, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oral vancomycin. It’s the best for C. diff. We’ll confirm with the test results tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, James. Your stool test came back positive for C. diff. That explains the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I figured. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your medical history, but we caught it early. You’re on the right treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling a procedure today to replace it. It’s called a GJ tube exchange. It’s quick and done with imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation—fentanyl and midazolam—so you’ll be relaxed. The team will monitor you the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi James. The procedure went well. Your new feeding tube is in the right place—down into the jejunum. It’s a low-profile one, so it should be more comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I use it right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s ready. We’ll start with small amounts to make sure you tolerate it. Your nurse will help you manage it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any improvement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is better. I haven’t vomited since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs are improving too. Your bicarbonate was low yesterday—16—which means you were a bit acidic. It’s up to 19 now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. And now that your tube is working, we can give you nutrition that way too, which helps balance things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked another stool sample today—still no parasites or other infections. That’s good. It means C. diff is likely the main issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just need to keep taking the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for 10 more days. It’s a 14-day course. Stopping early can cause it to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is back to baseline. Creatinine is 1.4 now. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too, especially with your history. But you’re responding well to fluids and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no vomiting in three days, and your appetite is improving. We’re going to try advancing your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat solid food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with soft foods—like toast and applesauce. If you do well, we’ll move to regular meals by tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the soft diet well. You’re now on a regular diet. How’s your stomach feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little bloated, but no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your gut is healing. We’ll keep the vancomycin going for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in two days, if all goes well. You’ll need to finish the antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need help with the feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your home nurse already manages your meds and care, so she’ll handle the tube feeds. We’ll send instructions and supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure you have everything you need. You should follow up with your liver and primary care teams in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. No signs of infection. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot stronger. Can I walk more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We encourage it. Just use your cane if you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge team confirmed home health services will continue. They’ll help with tube feeds and check-ins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your usual meds—tacrolimus, prednisone, loperamide for diarrhea, and your heart meds. We’re not adding anything new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take opium tincture too, for the chronic diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart that as needed, but only after finishing the vancomycin, to avoid interactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is approved. We’ll get the paperwork ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: finish all the vancomycin, watch for diarrhea returning, and call if you have fever or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see my doctor next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, James.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m all set. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay hydrated, keep using the tube as directed, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One thing—should I avoid any foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-fat, easy-to-digest foods for now—like rice, bananas, toast. Avoid spicy or greasy meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep up with your fluids—especially water and broth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You’re all set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.
